Inter-segment boundary artifacts are the underappreciated failure mode — when two documents are concatenated with a separator token, the model has no mechanism to suppress cross-document attention, so early tokens from document B can attend strongly to late tokens of document A despite being semantically unrelated, corrupting both KV cache states and retrieved content. The compounding effect is that retrieval accuracy doesn't degrade gracefully; it collapses non-monotonically, with sharp performance cliffs at specific context depths that reflect constructive interference between sink amplification, RoPE frequency aliasing, and segment-local attention pattern leakage.

When |m−n| exceeds the training context length, the high-frequency dimension pairs (those with small base wavelengths) complete multiple full rotations, making position 1000 and position 33768 geometrically identical in those subspaces — this is the aliasing. The damage is structurally non-uniform because attention scores are a sum across all dimension pairs: low-frequency subspaces (large base wavelengths) remain unaliased and continue contributing meaningful signal, while high-frequency subspaces inject random-phase noise that adds constructively or destructively depending on the specific (m,n) pair — producing retrieval errors rather than uniform suppression because some query-key pairs happen to receive constructive interference and score anomalously high. The practical failure mode is that a query token at position 80k can spuriously retrieve a key at position 12k not because they are semantically similar, but because their high-frequency phase components happen to align — a false positive that displaces the genuinely relevant key. This is precisely why "lost in the middle" retrieval failures (Liu et al., 2023) are position-structured rather than random: the spurious retrievals cluster around positions where phase aliasing creates constructive interference peaks, producing systematic rather than diffuse errors.

The "no change" encoding problem is a specific instance of the null signal degeneracy failure: if the anchor token sequence carries no semantic content distinguishing which constraint remained satisfied from any other constraint, attention heads routing to that anchor receive zero gradient signal during any fine-tuning and learn to treat it as a sink — behaviorally indistinguishable from the positional sink amplification at segment boundaries described earlier. The solution space requires distinguishing identity-preserving continuity from absence of information: rather than encoding "variable X unchanged," the anchor must encode "variable X holds value V at step N, verified against constraint C" — a confirmation token that carries the full state tuple even when the delta is zero, but structured so its key vector is maximally distant from the original encoding of that same state at position p₀ to avoid the superposition conflict. The invariant tracking case in constraint satisfaction is particularly acute because CSP reasoning requires the model to maintain a closed-world assumption across steps: the absence of a contradiction is meaningful, and systems like SatLM (Ye et al., 2023) that offload constraint checking to external solvers rather than encoding it in-context sidestep this problem entirely by externalizing the "no change" bookkeeping to a deterministic verifier. For purely in-context solutions, the most robust encoding is a monotonic step counter embedded in the anchor: [STEP=7, HOLDS=3, CHANGED=0] forces the model to attend to step identity first, making each anchor positionally unique by construction even when semantic content is identical across steps, which prevents the degenerate sink behavior by ensuring no two anchors share the same key-vector neighborhood. The primary failure at the interface boundary is grounding token misalignment: when the symbolic state machine returns a provably correct state vector, it must be serialized back into tokens and injected at a specific context position — and the transformer now treats that injection as a new document segment with its own positional encoding, reintroducing exactly the inter-segment boundary artifacts from the original problem, where the model's attention conflates the symbolic return value with nearby prose tokens rather than treating it as authoritative external state. Fine-tuning the transformer to interface with the symbolic component requires the model to learn a privileged attention pattern — heavily upweighting symbolic return tokens over same-window prose tokens — but positional encoding works against this because the symbolic injection at position p is geometrically similar to any other token at position p, and the model has no native mechanism to mark it as extra-contextual or authoritative without explicit architectural support like cross-attention to a separate symbolic memory stream. The pathology re-emerges specifically in multi-call interfaces: after the first symbolic query-response cycle, the response tokens sit at some position p₁; after the second cycle, at p₂; by the third or fourth call the model must retrieve and compare outputs from p₁, p₂, p₃ — which are now separated by hundreds of prose tokens — using the same degraded long-range attention that fails for ordinary retrieval, so the symbolic correctness guarantee is undermined not by the symbolic component but by the transformer's failure to reliably read its own tool outputs across distance. Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) documented a version of this: API call results injected mid-sequence were correctly retrieved when within ~200 tokens of the query point but showed sharp accuracy degradation beyond that, even when the retrieved value was unambiguous, consistent with high-frequency RoPE band degradation in the mesoscale window. The fine-tuning dynamic compounds this because gradient signal during training flows through the interface boundary — the model learns to predict tokens after a symbolic return, but the loss function doesn't penalize misreading the symbolic token itself, only downstream generation errors, so the model can achieve low training loss while systematically misattending to symbolic returns that occur beyond its reliable retrieval horizon. The resolution that works architecturally is positional isolation via attention masking: forcing all symbolic return tokens into a dedicated positional slot (position 0–K, always near-context) via a ring buffer or prefix cache, so their positional encoding never exceeds the training distribution — but this requires inference infrastructure that rewrites context positions dynamically, which conflicts with standard KV cache assumptions and has only been partially implemented in systems like MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023).
